# Baruch — The HESED Reader's Guide
**Guide by:** HESED (חֶסֶד — Lovingkindness)

---

## At a Glance
| | |
|---|---|
| **Author** | Unknown; pseudonymously attributed to Baruch son of Neriah, Jeremiah's secretary |
| **Date** | Composite work: parts as early as 3rd century BCE, final form c. 150–50 BCE |
| **Audience** | Diaspora Jews, likely in Babylon and/or Alexandria |
| **Genre** | Composite: liturgical prayer, wisdom hymn, prophetic consolation |
| **Timeline** | Fictional setting: Babylon after the destruction of Jerusalem (586 BCE) |
| **In One Sentence** | A composite book written in Jeremiah's shadow assembles the three voices of exile — confession, contemplation, and consolation — into a single theological statement that wisdom was lost with Jerusalem but can be found again through obedience to God's Torah. |

---

## The World Behind the Text

The book opens with a scene of striking pathos: Baruch, the loyal secretary of the prophet Jeremiah, reads a scroll to King Jeconiah and the exiles gathered by the River Sud in Babylon (1:1–4). The exiles weep and fast, collect money to send back to Jerusalem, and compose a prayer of confession. The scene is carefully modeled on Ezra 8–9 and Nehemiah 8–9 — the great post-exilic scenes of reading, weeping, and confession — and it invites the reader to understand this book as belonging to the literature of exile: texts written to help a displaced people make theological sense of catastrophic loss.

The Baruch of history was a real person — the scribe who wrote down Jeremiah's dictated words (Jer 36), who accompanied the prophet, who was given a personal oracle of consolation (Jer 45). He was a figure closely associated with the most terrible period of Judean history, the generation that witnessed the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem and the end of the Davidic monarchy. For a later author writing for communities that experienced their own forms of dispossession and cultural threat — whether under Seleucid Greek rule in the second century or under Roman dominance in the first — the name "Baruch" was a natural pseudonym. It placed the text in the tradition of those who had survived the worst and still believed.

The composite nature of the book is visible to any careful reader. Chapter 1:1–3:8 is written in prose and reads as liturgical penitential prayer — formal, structured, echoing the great confession prayers of Ezra and Nehemiah and Daniel 9. Chapters 3:9–4:4 shift suddenly into the elevated poetic register of wisdom hymn, comparable to Job 28 and Proverbs 8. Chapters 4:5–5:9 shift again into prophetic consolation, with a voice that closely imitates Deutero-Isaiah (Isaiah 40–55). Most scholars believe these sections were composed separately and assembled by a later editor, perhaps in the second or first century BCE. The seams show — but they also reveal the editor's intention: all three modes of response to exile belong together. Confession without contemplation is empty; contemplation without consolation is cold; consolation without confession is cheap.

---

## Why This Book Was Written

The book's central theological claim is stated with memorable precision at the hinge point between the prayer section and the wisdom hymn: "Why is it, O Israel, why is it that you are in the land of your enemies, that you are growing old in a foreign country, that you are defiled with the dead, that you are counted among those who go down to Hades? You have forsaken the fountain of wisdom" (3:10–12). This is not a historical inquiry — it is a theological diagnosis. Exile is the consequence of forsaking Wisdom, and Wisdom is identified, in the hymn's stunning conclusion, with the Torah that God gave to Jacob: "She is the book of the commandments of God, the law that endures forever. All who hold her fast will live, and those who forsake her will die" (4:1).

This identification of cosmic Wisdom with Torah — a move also made in Sirach 24 and elaborated further in later rabbinic thought — is the theological core of the book. The opening sections explain how Israel came to be in exile (by abandoning Wisdom/Torah, by sinning, by refusing to listen to the prophets). The middle section celebrates Wisdom as the most precious thing in the cosmos, inaccessible to human searching, given by God alone to Israel. The closing sections promise that God has not abandoned exiled Israel, that the same God who scattered will gather, that the children will return to the mother city from every direction under the sky.

The book was written, in all its composite parts, to hold a community together under the pressure of dispossession. It names the sin honestly (the confession sections are unflinching in their self-indictment) while refusing to let that honest self-accounting become despair. The movement of the book is the movement the author believes the community must make: from the acknowledgment of failure, through the contemplation of what was lost, to the reception of the promise that loss is not the final word.

---

## How to Read This Book

Baruch is a short book — six chapters in most reckonings, though some traditions count the Letter of Jeremiah as Baruch 6 — and it can be read in a single sitting. But it is a book that rewards reading in three stages, corresponding to its three distinct literary movements.

The opening prayer (1:15–3:8) should be read in the tradition of the great Jewish communal confession prayers — Daniel 9, Ezra 9, Nehemiah 9. These prayers follow a recognizable structure: acknowledgment of God's righteousness, acknowledgment of the community's sin, recitation of specific failures, and plea for mercy. Reading Baruch's prayer alongside Daniel 9 is illuminating: both are clearly drawing on a shared liturgical tradition, and comparing them reveals both the common template and the individual emphases of each.

The wisdom hymn (3:9–4:4) should be read slowly, as poetry. It begins with a rhetorical question (why are you in exile?) and moves through a meditation on the inaccessibility of Wisdom to human searching — the giants could not find her, the merchants of Merran and Teman did not know her, even the practitioners of astrology in Babylon could not locate her (3:17–23). The hymn climaxes with the declaration that only God knows where Wisdom is, and God gave her to Israel. The final verses (4:1–4) identify Wisdom with Torah and call Israel blessed above all people. This is one of the great wisdom poems of the Jewish tradition, comparable in ambition and beauty to the better-known Proverbs 8 and Job 28.

The consolation section (4:5–5:9) shifts to a maternal voice — Jerusalem personified as a mother, speaking to her scattered children — that has obvious affinities with the City of Jerusalem sections in Lamentations and the "Daughter Zion" passages in Deutero-Isaiah. Jerusalem mourns, then comforts, then looks for the return of her children with almost frantic hope. The short hymn that closes the book (chapter 5) — "Take off the garment of your sorrow and affliction, O Jerusalem, and put on forever the beauty of the glory from God" — is one of the finest short lyrics in the deuterocanonical corpus.

---

## The Threads — How This Book Connects

**Jeremiah (the book's haunting presence throughout):** Baruch is, at every level, a response to the Book of Jeremiah. The author writes in the name of Jeremiah's scribe, echoes Jeremiah's prose style in the prayer sections, and situates the book in the Babylonian exile that Jeremiah predicted and mourned. Bar 1:15–2:19 is so closely parallel to portions of Jeremiah 32 and 44 that some scholars have proposed direct literary dependence. The book is, in a sense, the theological sequel that the Book of Jeremiah never wrote: while Jeremiah ends in ambiguity and grief, Baruch moves toward consolation.

**Daniel 9 (penitential prayer tradition):** The great confession prayer in Daniel 9:4–19 and the prayer in Baruch 1:15–3:8 are so structurally similar — and share so much specific language — that they are almost certainly drawing on a common liturgical tradition of communal confession prayer. Whether one borrowed from the other, or both from a common source, they illuminate each other beautifully when read together.

**Job 28 and Proverbs 8 (Wisdom hymn tradition):** The wisdom hymn in Baruch 3:9–4:4 stands in direct dialogue with the "Where shall Wisdom be found?" meditation in Job 28 and the Praise of Wisdom in Proverbs 8. In all three texts, Wisdom is a cosmic figure inaccessible to human searching; in all three, she is available only through the gift of God. Baruch makes the specific move of identifying Wisdom with Torah, which Job 28 does implicitly ("the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom") and Proverbs 8 does not quite make.

**Deutero-Isaiah (Isaiah 40–55, consolation of exile):** The closing consolation section of Baruch is saturated with the imagery and theology of Isaiah 40–55: the return of the exiles, the transformation of the landscape for their journey, Jerusalem looking up to see her children coming from East and West, the glory of the Lord as the light that guides them. Baruch 5:1–9 is, in many ways, a lyric condensation of Isaiah 40–55's consolation vision. Reading them together shows how the author understood his own work: not as replacing Deutero-Isaiah's vision but as re-presenting it for a new generation.

**Sirach 24 (Wisdom = Torah identification):** Ben Sira's great wisdom poem in Sirach 24 makes the same identification — Wisdom sought a dwelling, and God told her to dwell in Israel, in the Torah. Baruch 3:9–4:4 and Sirach 24 are the two most explicit pre-Christian formulations of this equation, and both are important background for understanding John 1's claim that the Logos "became flesh and dwelt among us."

**Bar 3:37 and the Incarnation:** The verse "Afterward she appeared on earth and lived with human beings" (Bar 3:37) has been read by Christian interpreters since the second century as a reference to the Incarnation — Wisdom/the divine Word taking human form. In its original context, "she" almost certainly refers to Wisdom as given to Israel in the Torah. But the verse's language is striking enough that early Christian writers (Irenaeus, Tertullian, Origen) quoted it as a direct prophecy of Christ. The verse stands as one of the deuterocanonical texts most important to Christian theological development, whatever its original meaning.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

The composite nature of Baruch is both its weakness and its strength, and modern readers accustomed to unified authorial voices may find the book's shifts in style jarring rather than theologically productive. The jarring is worth attending to. The editor who assembled these three sections was making a claim: that confession, contemplation, and consolation are all necessary, and that none of them can stand alone. The prayer without the wisdom hymn would be mere self-flagellation. The wisdom hymn without the consolation would be beautiful but cold. The consolation without the confession would ring hollow. The composite structure is itself a theological statement.

The text's use of feminine personification for Jerusalem and for Wisdom is one of its most powerful features and one that modern translations sometimes mute. In Baruch 4–5, Jerusalem speaks as a mother, mourning her children with the specificity of maternal grief, then rising to look for their return with the urgency of a parent who cannot stop watching the horizon. This is not merely decorative — it is a profound theological move, placing the suffering of exile within the framework of a relationship, a love that cannot be extinguished by distance or time.

The liturgical use of Baruch in early Christian communities is documented and significant. Portions of Baruch — particularly the consolation sections — were read in Holy Saturday liturgies, as texts that held the space of waiting between death and resurrection. The Easter Vigil use of Baruch 3:9–15 and 3:32–4:4 in the Roman Catholic rite continues to this day. Modern Protestant readers encountering this text for the first time may not realize that it has been shaping the theological imagination of Christian worship for nearly two millennia.

---

## Why This Book Isn't in Your Bible

Like many deuterocanonical texts, Baruch was written and circulated in Greek, and no Hebrew original has been recovered for the book as a whole (though some scholars believe portions of chapters 1–3 may have been translated from a Hebrew or Aramaic source). Its exclusion from the Hebrew Tanakh followed from the same principle that governed the exclusion of other Greek-language Jewish texts: the emerging Hebrew canon was Hebrew.

The book's status in early Christianity was variable. Some Church Fathers treated it as canonical and quoted it as "Jeremiah" — because of its connection to Jeremiah and its placement after Jeremiah in some manuscripts. Others distinguished it. The Vulgate included Baruch (and the Letter of Jeremiah as its sixth chapter), and it was listed among the deuterocanonical books defined as canonical by the Council of Trent in 1546.

Protestant reformers returned to the Hebrew canon principle and placed Baruch in the Apocrypha, where it remains in editions of the King James Bible that include the Apocrypha. It is not included in most Protestant Old Testaments today. Eastern Orthodox Christianity treats it as fully canonical.

---

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 586 BCE | Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem — the historical event behind the book's setting |
| 582 BCE | Gedaliah assassinated; flight to Egypt (Jer 43); traditional date of Baruch accompanying Jeremiah |
| c. 250–200 BCE | Probable composition of the earliest sections of Baruch |
| c. 200–150 BCE | Sirach composed — parallel wisdom tradition for comparison (Sirach 24 = Baruch 3:9–4:4) |
| c. 165–50 BCE | Most likely period for the final assembly of Baruch's composite sections |
| c. 100 BCE | Book present in Greek Septuagint tradition |
| 2nd century CE | Irenaeus, Tertullian quote Baruch 3:37 as Incarnation prophecy |
| c. 382–405 CE | Jerome's Vulgate includes Baruch; sometimes counted as part of Jeremiah |
| 1546 CE | Council of Trent formally defines Baruch as deuterocanonical for Roman Catholics |
| 1611 CE | King James Bible includes Baruch in the Apocrypha section |
| Present | Baruch 3:9–4:4 read at the Easter Vigil in the Roman Catholic liturgy |
